Yes, they certainly do. The hon. member can check the figures, if he likes. Ten years ago, our total trade amounted to $10 billion and our deficit in manufactured goods was about $3 billion. In 1977, our total trade was $44 billion- a substantial increase-and there was an increase in the deficit in manufactured goods. But in looking at manufactured and semi-processed goods we find that there has been a tremendous increase in our trade with the world. In fact, two-thirds of Canada's exports or in manufactured and semi-processed goods, not raw materials, as members of the opposition have sometimes said in the House.
In 1977, looking at agricultural commodities alone, less than 10 per cent of our total trade was in agricultural commodities. Many people in western Canada believe that we survive as a trading nation mainly because of our wheat sales. In fact, less than 10 per cent of our total sales are in agricultural commodities and less than 20 per cent of our total exports are of natural gas, oil and minerals. So if you take a look at those figures you see that the other portion is manufactured goods and semi-processed goods, including forest products, an industry which is thriving in the province of British Columbia. This gives you an idea of what the total trade picture is.
How does EDC assist total trade? Much has been said about their excessive demand for money in this legislation and it is suggested that we are granting EDC too much money because hon. members opposite fear that somehow or other EDC will squander it and help a host of communist countries. First of all, I want to make it abundantly clear that EDC is helping the Canadian manufacturing industry in all parts of Canada. It will certainly help the Avalon Company. If it wants help, it can come to EDC and receive that help. EDC has assisted Versatile Manufacturing Limited in Winnipeg, shipyards on both the east and west coasts, and the mining and nickel industries of Ontario. In fact, they have assisted substantially the nickel industry.
Many speakers have expressed concern about the fact that we are selling pulp mills to Poland and the United States, as well as steel mills to the United States. This helps Canada maintain its expertise in the development of efficient pulp mills. Why are Canadian steel mills far more efficient than
[Mr. Horner.)
American ones? It is because they are more modern, and we have been able to take advantage of new technological advances in the steel industry. Why are Canadian slaughtering houses and packing plants more modern than many others? It is because they are new and up to date. As I once said in this House, we were able to sell even a sausage-making machine to Germany. The Germans found it hard to believe that we could manufacture a better machine than they could.
Canada's ability to sell pulp mills, steel mills and packing plants enables us to maintain our position as a leader in those industries. No matter how much protection the opposition wants our industries to have, one must realize that we are living in a fiercely competitive world. Our entire survival depends upon our ability to compete. Whether a pulp mill is in Poland or the United States, we must be able to compete with it. Our ability to compete will be determined by the source of our raw materials, efficiency in handling those raw materials, as well as the speed of the transportation system which allows us to move processed and semi-processed products to the markets of the world. We must recognize that. We cannot say, "Do not finance a steel mill or a pulp mill in the United States because they will be competing against us someday". Of course the competition will be there. If we had not invested in the American pulp mill, Finland would have. Finland was ready and able to do it.
We have heard a great deal about the Export Development Corporation and its extensive use of money. In order to provide hon. members with some idea of the value of support which EDC has given to the Candian gross national product, I should like to point out that in Canada it amounts to a little over 1 per cent. If one compares that with all other countries, one would have some idea whether EDC is requesting something which is outlandish or too large. For example, in Germany the support is 2 per cent of the gross national product, in Italy it is 2 per cent, in Japan it is over 5 per cent, in Great Britain it is over 5 per cent, and in France it is 7.5 per cent. In fact, EDC assists in 5 per cent or less of our total exports. If someone wanted to take a very negative position and suggest that we have no confidence in Canada's ability to export, then 1 suppose he should say that EDC is requesting too much money. If one wanted to be negative in one's thinking, one could adopt that idea, but certainly it is not my belief.
Canada's ability to export goods is growing at a great rate. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) pointed out, the Middle East is becoming quite credit worthy, to put it mildly. It has developed and increased its oil reserves, and is now charging a high price for those reserves. The Middle East wants the commodities which Canadians have become accustomed to. It wants to buy those commodities, and we are in the business of selling them. One can say that the Middle East does not require any assistance in purchasing our commodities because of its oil reserves. If a person has a good creditworthiness, then he extends his credit in all directions. That is what many countries are doing. Certainly that will expand our export markets in the next five years particularly.

I would like now to refer specifically to the bill before this House. Although I am a new member of less than ten hours' formal standing, I have had some opportunity to become acquainted with this debate. This bill asks basically four things of the House. First, it asks for authority to increase government borrowing by $7 billion during this fiscal year; second, authority to increase government borrowing by an additional $10 billion in the next fiscal year; third, explicit authority to place all or part of that borrowing in foreign markets; and fourth, explicit authority to maintain all previously authorized borrowings in perpetuity, if the government chooses, as a charge against the people of Canada.

Seven months and three days later, the minister informs the House of the need for an additional $7 billion-a 33 per cent increase over the total cash needs he forecast for two years.

Presumably that $300 million is covered by this request, but in addition he suddenly discovered a need for an additional $6.7 billion. He still refuses to give budgetary deficit forecasts when the most conservative figures-and I use that adjective deliberately-indicate a minimum $13 billion deficit which could soar to $15 billion to $16 billion. This government has a credibility problem, and it need look no further than this sort of behaviour for the reason.

Certainly, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will be permitted to proceed with the point. 1 would like to set the record straight and then the matter can be discussed.
By virtue of relatively recent changes in our procedures, we have transferred the consideration or the calling of motions pursuant to Standing Order 43 to the beginning of the day, prior to the question period.
This problem has arisen once or twice in the past. On those rare occasions when the House does give its consent that the motion be presented, the question is put. The question is not, as all hon. members will know, when an application is made pursuant to Standing Order 43, for the passage of the motion, but simply for the putting of the question, for there is no authority to put a motion at that hour of the day, or, for that matter, at any time by a private member, outside of the private members' hour. Therefore authority is sought, pursuant to Standing Order 43, to put the question, and the question being asked is not the consent of the House to pass the motion, but the consent of the House to put the motion.
Occasionally the House gives it consent, as it did today. Therefore, when the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) put the question earlier, he was seeking the consent of the House that his motion be put, and since the House gave its consent, the motion was put. The motion then becomes debatable, and it is the duty of the Chair therefore to call the motion for debate: "Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?" Any members then rising obviously must be recognized by the Chair for participation in the debate. Today, the only member who was rising at the time of the calling of the question was the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts). At 2.15 a confrontation, or collision, occurs between that rule pursuant to Standing Order 43, and that practice in another standing order which prescribes that the question period shall begin at 2.15 and continue until three o'clock.
1 want to refer hon. members to Standing Order 45(2) which reads:
When a debate on any motion made prior to the reading of the orders of the day is adjourned or interrupted, the order for resumption of the same shall be transferred to and considered under government orders.
It seems to me that we had two choices at 2.15. One of them was, by virtue of having put a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43, to set aside the question period at 2.15 because the debate was under way. Obviously the danger with that is that if we set aside the question period and the debate carries on- for example, until three o'clock or later-we would need the consent of the House to restore the question period. So, the risk is that if we continue with the debate at 2.15 we wipe out

the question period, to which, I am sure, all hon. members would be opposed.

BasePK: 3176170

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the question I put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) yesterday was concerned with Great Britain's involvement in the supplying of arms and munitions to certain African states in high tension areas where such "aid" can only result in further violence and bloodshed. I wanted to know particularly whether the Canadian government has commented in any way to the United Kingdom with regard to this volatile situation, and the minister replied rather lamely in the negative. This does appear to be a case of silence being consent.
At any rate, the government does not appear to object to Britain involving herself in these African atrocities in precisely the same manner as the Russians and the Cubans, placing modern weaponry in the hands of tribal warriors whose main goal these days seems to be to kill anyone who disagrees with them, or even anyone they suspect might disagree with them.
It is a dangerous game, one which the communists have been playing for a long time in Africa and elsewhere. Britain and, by association, other members of the Commonwealth would be most unwise to get into this lopsided chess game at which the Russians are past masters. In that part of the world today, Britain is sadly outnumbered and it is foolhardy to think that sending a few guns-though in this case it is much more serious because we are talking about surface-to-air missiles and other such pieces of sophisticated equipment-to Zambia is going to thwart any plans being engineered by the communists.
Adjournment Debate
An arms build-up in Africa can only lead to tribal wars and genocide; civil wars, if you like. These in turn can spread across state borders, eventually involving any number of African states. Since Cuba has been highly visible in African affairs for some time-and it appears that our government has co-operated with Cuba in its efforts to get arms and men to that troubled continent in the past by allowing their war materiel to land in this country en route to Africa-and since it is common knowledge that the Soviet Union has been supplying various states and factions with war materiel for years, this is no game for the British who have enough problems at home and in Ireland.
By its commonwealth association and by its silent consent, the Canadian government is involving itself in African affairs along with Britain. This is foolhardy enough in itself, but really foolish when you stop to think of the odds stacked against anyone who confronts communist-backed forces in that part of the world now.
This government has been pouring money hand over fist into African countries, supposedly to feed starving millions of people. How much of that money is feeding the people and how much of it is buying bullets, bombs and back-up material from the communists? How much of that money is killing the very people it was intended to keep alive?
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that the World Council of Churches has been giving aid to these terrorists. I was amazed on Sunday night to see the Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada on television admitting that he was only going by his conscience and was not concerned with what was actually going on. He had not made any effort to visit the area. It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that 95 per cent of the people killed in Rhodesia by the guerrillas invading from Zambia are black people.
The minister said earlier today that he would need more specific information on Britain's involvement in African affairs. All he needs to do is read the same newspapers we all have access to. But he prefers to sit, wait for word from London, hoping and praying nervously all the while that these nasty things will pass away and Africa will settle down to a peaceful, pastoral picture once again. It seems to me he is proceeding in a very naive way.
I say to the minister that African people, in one part of that continent or another, have not known true peace in this entire century. There has always been some big nation from Europe sticking its thumb in to see what it could come up with. And Britain is back into the act, not as the empire builder she once was, but as a relatively minor member of a gang of misdirected moderns who will achieve nothing there but the building of a gigantic powder keg.
We must not forget that the Middle East problem also involves part of Africa-a big part of Africa in the north. So it is all part of the same grandiose chess game and it becomes increasingly and dangerously unstable every time one more non-African nation tries to get into the act.

October 31, 1978
Adjournment Debate
If Canada is seen to approve, silently or otherwise, British involvement in African affairs, then this country's position is jeopardized, whether we are seen as aligning ourselves with communist aggressors or simply doing nothing to persuade Britain from doing just that. If his government, as the minister says, really believes this kind of arms escalation must be brought to an end, then let us have some action on at least some strong words on the subject, not just a mouthful of excuses.

BasePK: 3176171

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) stated in the House on October 30 that he had had no conversations with the British Foreign Secretary regarding Britain's decision to send military supplies to Zambia. We would not, indeed, expect the British government to consult us on its transactions with a sovereign fellow member of the Commonwealth concerning its defence needs.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs added that, when he had more specific information, he would consider whether it was useful to the House to give a more detailed response. We are seeking confirmation of press and other reports that the military equipment sent to Zambia is for Zambia's defence needs, particularly air defence. According to reports, the supplies have included communications equipment, mine detectors and anti-aircraft guns, with the possibility of ground-to-air missiles to follow, and they have been supplied on condition that they are not handed on to the guerilla forces.
We also understand from reports that Dr. Owen has stated that there was no question of stationing British troops or aircraft in Zambia or of sending any equipment that could be used for any purpose other than the protection of Zambia.
As all hon. members will realize, the actions of the British government are related to the vexing Rhodesian question. For too many years the repressive Rhodesian regime has illegally exercised power in defiance of the international community and the situation has been in the forefront of unsolved international problems. The unacceptability of the illegal regime's policies and its intransigence in the face of international efforts to find solutions have through the years severely affected the neighbouring states. Incursions such as took place in recent weeks and particularly the raids into Zambia point up the need for all parties to get together to discuss peaceful ways to settle the affair without delay. Zambia is particularly vulnerable, both militarily and economically, to Rhodesian actions. It is unable to protect itself from the operation of the illegal regime's security forces. In addition, it has had to open its border to permit transhipment of vital supplies of fertilizer through Rhodesia.
It appears from all reports that the military supplies are indeed of a defensive nature and intended only for Zambia's defence should it be attacked. Until we have confirmation of the reports, however, we can make no further comment.

Mr. Speaker, I would have to agree with the views expressed by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn). The number of opportunities for the House to consider the activities of the Canadian Transport Commission or even of the Department of Transport in depth are few and far between, and it looks as though they will be unusually limited this session.
There are a number of items which should be considered, both by the department and by the commission. Applications such as those referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) come before the Canadian Transport Commission without any onus upon the applicant for abandonment of service to prove that there is in fact no business. There is no onus upon the applicant to prove that he or she has made a proper effort to obtain the business which might be available in the area to be abandoned. There is no onus upon the Canadian Transport Commission to consider seriously the human, industrial or social needs for a particular service and to say in an unqualified way that the carrier must continue the service which he has suggested he should abandon.
I am particularly concerned about the aspect of the situation in which the carrier is not requested to indicate how much business is in the area and what effort the carrier has made to obtain that business. It appears to the public that the carrier very often may deliberately reduce service to a level which makes it totally unacceptable to the shipper or passenger. Having become totally unacceptable, it is of course not properly patronized, and the application for abandonment of the particular service automatically follows.
I think the questions which I raised in the House today put an exclamation mark after this procedure, over which the government apparently has no control or, if the government and the CTC do have control, the minister of many years is not prepared at this moment to state what element of control they do have. A carrier may be permitted to abandon a service, the transportation of a product, without application to the CTC, and this is a very dangerous situation.
I understand the reasons for the presentation of this bill, but I must say that because it deals with an isolated instance it cannot be used as an instrument to justify the limitation of the power of the CTC to change its position. Nor can it justify itself on a national basis because it cites a specific instance. My sympathies are with the applicant and with the residents of Windsor-Walkerville who are concerned about this problem, but I would not like to see this matter considered in the committee as an individual case with relation to the CTC, its decisions and what rights of appeal there are. I would like to see this bill go to the committee so that there can be an opportunity to consider the general transportation problems of Canada and the decisions which are being made by the CTC.

I would like this subject matter to go to the committee so that we might get a proper delineation of the opportunity to appeal to the CTC when service is not officially suspended but in practice is, as is the case with the CPR and the potato industry in the province of New Brunswick, and as is that case with respect to perishable food products and processed products in the Dominion of Canada. There has been a virtual withdrawal by the railroad systems from their responsibility to transport these products.
If this bill were to go to committee and if the government permitted a broad study of the responsibilities of the railroads, the authority of the minister and the authority of the CTC so that these things might be spelled out, the bill might then be amended, not just as it refers to the CTC and a specific case but, rather, as it refers to transportation problems in Canada generally. I strongly recommend that this bill go to a committee on that basis. It would be unfortunate if it went to committee and was considered only with respect to a specific instance because the subject matter is much broader than that. I do not offer any prejudice to the specific instance outlined in this bill, but I do want to use it as an example of a broad transportation problem in all of Canada.
If the bill could go to the committee in that context, I think we could have a very proper discussion on how the government, the CTC and the railroad structure of Canada could combine to give better service on a broad basis and assure all Canadians that where service is essential the railroads shall be obligated to continue that service.

Mr. Speaker, you will undoubtedly recall that on October 20 I raised a point of order on a motion which was attempted to be put before the House by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees). I rose
Point of Order-Mr. MacEachen on that occasion because it seemed to me that that that particular motion was an excellent example of the extent to which proceedings under Standing Order 43 had developed in the House of Commons. I use the word "developed" when I really mean the word "deteriorated." I believe it is very appropriate to draw attention to the concerns which we on this side of the House feel with respect to the operation of Standing Order 43.
The history of the Standing Order is straightforward. It was first introduced in 1867. It was revised in 1927 by the addition of the requirement of urgency for seeking unanimous consent to put motions without prior notice. It is interesting to recall that until 1969 the rule was used sparingly, but following that year, for some inexplicable reason-maybe not so inexplicable-there suddenly developed in Canada a flood of urgent and pressing matters.
In 1975 the procedure committee decide to revise Standing Order 43 by providing a 15-minute limit, and the proceeding was placed before the question period. That recommendation of the procedure committee was concurred in without debate or amendment. As Your Honour has indicated, the time limit introduced in 1975 introduced a self-policing feature. Requests for unanimous consent under Standing Order 43 cannot take more than 15 minutes, and presumably hon. members are encouraged by their colleagues to restrict their motions to genuinely urgent matters, and not to waste time with frivolous motions.
The theory that Standing Order 43 motions are restricted to genuinely urgent matters because of the limited time period has not proved valid. All the 15-minute period has policed is the period itself, and it has had little affect on what happens within that period. I believe that the content of the motions now proposed requires critical attention on the part of members of the House and, with due respect, of the Chair as well.
It is not my intention to limit the use of Standing Order 43. Fifteen minutes are set aside for private members to use this proceeding, and as far as I am concerned it can be used to the maximum. What I am concerned about is the misuse of Standing Order 43. When hon. members rise under Standing Order 43, they are asking the House to waive the normal requirement for 48 hours' notice to put motions before the House, on the ground that the matters involved are of pressing and urgent necessity.
The first requirement is that a matter must be so urgent and so pressing that the House will waive notice, and the motion can be put before the House with consent. I submit that the rule has not been used properly because hon. members have ignored the requirement of urgency. They have misused the rule by delivering speeches in the guise of lengthy preambles and lengthy motions. They have misused the rule by proposing frivolous motions. I can give examples.
Hon. members have misused the rule by making unsubstantiated allegations which cannot be replied to without debate, which is not normally possible and which, if it were possible, would waste valuable time of the House which could otherwise be used for public business.

November 6, 1978
Point of Order-Mr. MacEachen
The operation of the Standing Order has suffered greatly because its basic procedural purpose has been ignored regularly. Motions under this Standing Order must be of such urgency as to warrant asking the House to waive the normal notice requirement and to interrupt the normal order of business so that they can be considered. If a motion does not meet the criterion of urgency, it should be dealt with under the normal rules of the House by way of private members' motions, with 48 hours' notice. The result of the failure to observe the rule of urgency is that genuinely urgent matters which might deserve consideration are submerged or drowned in a flood of nonurgent, frivolous, and blatantly argumentative motions. This is a very troubling feature of these motions.
Let us consider, for example, the motion put by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) last Monday. He raised the question of social insurance numbers. That matter has been in the political atmosphere since 1965 at least, and it could hardly be described as an urgent and pressing matter. But within the preamble and within the motion itself there are a number of what I would regard as argumentative, unsubstantiated, and unfounded allegations.
The hon. member alleges that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is actively encouraging the expanded use of social insurance numbers by all levels of government, contrary to longstanding commitments by the Government of Canada. These are points of view with which we disagree. I have no objection to the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar stating his views on this point-views with which I and other members of the House disagree-but when do we have an opportunity under this proceeding to say that we do not agree and that these are not the facts as we see them?
Within the motions and within the lengthy preambles all sorts of argumentation are contained, with no opportunity for hon. members on this side of the House to state the facts as they see them. I regard this as a very fundamental weakness of the present proceeding, that it is possible, under the guise of alleged urgency and pressing necessity, to put forward argument, debate and partisanship, all of which is quite acceptable provided there is an opportunity to deal with it by members of the House who disagree with the point of view that is stated.

BasePK: 3177354

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I want to pursue the issue of the reduction of moneys for, and the closure of, forestry research laboratories brought about by the federal government. I have raised this issue on a number of occasions. On October 19 I put the specific question to the minister, and I did so again today.
It is my contention that the government's restraint program is both arbitrary and irrational as it pertains to Canadian forestry services. What we have seen is that cutbacks and the elimination of important government services, because of the general restraint program, are having a devastating effect on the morale and the work of people in government forestry research laboratories.
Last August, out of the blue, the Department of the Environment was told to cut its expenditures by $40.5 million, including $11.7 million from its science support programs. This was a result of the general restraint program of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). The closure of forests research stations is supposed to save the government $2 million, and the transfer of two forests products labs to the private sector will supposedly result in another $3.3 million saving. As I pointed out earlier today during the question period, because of tax deductions the saving in reality will only amount to about $800,000. The key question before this House is, will the reduction in government research and development and the privatizing of government laboratories have a beneficial effect on the forestry industry of Canada?
Why is the forestry industry so important, Mr. Speaker? We find that one of every ten Canadian jobs is connected with forest products, and these products sell for $12 billion, or 14 per cent of our over-all manufactured goods. In other words, the forestry industry is a crucial sector in Canada. Therefore, it is important that this industry be enhanced in any way possible.
One of the very important long-range effects on that industry is related to the level of research and development in this country. The private sector in the past has relied very heavily on government research and development. In reality, Mr. Speaker, when you look at the figures, the record of the private sector in research and development in forestry has been a very dismal one. For example, in 1975 the wood products industry invested only .31 cents per dollar of shipment revenue on research and development compared to 2.5 cents per dollar by the electrical products industry. As a result, this low research and development expenditure has meant a lower productivity and employment rate in the forestry industry compared to
November 6, 1978

other sectors of the economy which spent much more on research and development.
When we look at research further, we find that in the private sector large companies carry out research that is mainly geared to design and marketing. This is quite natural because it enhances or maximizes their profits. The 8,000 small companies in the forestry sector hardly spend any money on research and development as they are small family affairs and cannot afford to. Therefore it is left to the government to fill the void. It is the government labs that work at the conceptual stage, bringing an idea along to the point where the private sector can take it over at the marketing and productivity stage.
For example, it has been government work that has led us to further development of non-toxic treatment of wood chips and a safer method of toxic effluent disposal. They have done tremendous work, for example, in a lab in my constituency on control of the spruce budworm. In other words, the role of government labs is crucial to the future well-being of our forestry industry.
What I regret is that this Liberal government, listening to Conservative cries for government restraint, has further arbitrarily cut back on procedures, undermining the forest industry. Its approach is irrational and arbitrary. We have seen, for example, the Petawawa forest station, that has been working for over 60 years doing world renowned research, being made the subject of cutback. The minister first announced it was going to be closed, but because of public outcry and public uproar from the scientific community the government reversed its decision. In the process of reversing its decision and keeping the Petawawa base open, the government caused a catastrophe in two other areas, the fire research centre and the forest management centre in Ottawa. One hundred employees were told out of the blue that in order to keep Petawawa open half of them would lose their jobs, the budget would be cut in half and that the other 50 would be transferred to Petawawa . All this was in light of study after study which showed the necessity for keeping those two institutes here in Ottawa close by the other agencies which they deal with, such as the National Research Council.
The government's approach makes no sense. There is no scientific rational basis for their flip-flop in policy, this arbitrary cuback and this ridiculous privatization which will not do the industry any good in the long run, for reasons which 1 have described.
I appeal to the parliamentary secretary and to the minister that if they are concerned about the state of research and development in the forestry industry in Canada, they should
Adjournment Debate
keep Petawawa open with a full complement and reverse their decision to close the two labs in Ottawa and transfer them to Petawawa. Surely, if the minister believes in the importance of research and development, he will reverse this irrational, arbitrary and unproductive decision.

BasePK: 3177355

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, of all the members in this House I can say to the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) that I totally agree with his remarks, being one who has been associated with one of the largest pulp and paper companies in the world, MacMillan Bloedel, for the past 35 years. I agree that the forestry industry is a vital part of the Canadian economy and that a vigorous research program is essential to assure its future.
The minister regrets that any reduction in the budget of the Canadian Forestry Service has to be made. However, the Department of Environment was required to reduce its budget by $40 million plus, as the hon. member has mentioned. A reduction of that magnitude means that no one element of the department could remain untouched. Every effort was made to make the cuts in such a way that the high levels of service and essential research can be maintained.
It should be noted that part of the government's intention in cutting the departmental budget was to provide funds for more immediate economic stimulation measures. Some $15 to $20 million of these funds annually will be channelled into joint projects with the provinces to improve forest management. These joint projects will be conducted under agreements between the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and provincial agencies. Environment Canada, through the Canadian Forestry Service, will provide technical and scientific input and advice.
As for the matter of privatization of the forest products laboratories, this has been under consideration for quite some time. In fact, the Canadian Forestry Advisory Council recommended in its 1973 report to the minister of the environment at that time that these laboratories be taken over by private industry. As the minister has stated before in this House, the total budget for these two laboratories was $7.3 million. If privatization were to become a reality, the continuing federal contribution of $4 million per year to the support of these laboratories would ensure the maintenance of a long-term research and development program.

So I think the same sort of thing will apply here.

I added my last comment because I was very much afraid that someone might bring up something I said 12 years ago. I was afraid someone would have it tucked up his sleeve, ready to trot out before the House.
Recently the government announced that it was going to cut back on public services. The Prime Minister came out with a great big axe in his hand. I presume he did not tell anyone about it. He came out looking like Henry VIII, chopping off ladies' heads, and saying, "Off with their heads, off with their heads". In the meantime, the heads are not rolling rapidly, nor should they roll rapidly. By the time you get through that exercise you really have not changed very much.
There is room and there is need for scrutiny in the public sector. All of us have some private and pet horror stories about what goes on in the public sector, or all of us should have, and some of us have stories about what goes on in the private sector. These things can only be handled on a day to day and consistent basis with a determination to make the public sector work. This is part of the problem.
If you wonder why bureaucracy is the way it is, and why there is less concern about the public sector than there should be, it is because governments, federal governments at any rate, up until the present time have had a kind of death wish. Sometimes one feels it really does not want the public sector to work. Like my friend, the hon. member for York-Simcoe, instead of putting their very considerable talents to work trying to figure out how to make Petro-Can of more service to the Canadian people, hon. members are busily trying to destroy Petro-Can. Like that hon. member, hon. members in that part of the House do not want Petro-Can to work because that would put a lie to the belief which is currently popular among members of the Conservative party. I say "currently" because things were not always that way. Many good endeavours have come from the Conservative party in its better days.
One of the great challenges of the future is not so much related to whether there should be more or less public involvement. I do not think it is possible any more in the kind of world we live in, and with the kind of future we foresee, for the government to get out of involvement in the economy. No government can divorce itself from that involvement. Quite to the contrary, there is an increasing need for the government to be involved in managing the economy. What is critical is not the extent to which the government is involved in the economy, but the extent to which people in public life ensure that the public sector always performs efficiently and humanely.
Because of our concern about the need for public investment and government leadership in the public sector, I move,
November 17, 1978

seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-

Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat embarrassed in answering my friend, my colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), as I have before me an answer written in the other official language, so I must answer in that language and I hope he will excuse me for that.

As the hon. member has indicated, unemployment in Canada has recently been at a level of 8.5 per cent of the labour force. However, it should be noted that in October the unemployment rate dropped to a seasonally adjusted rate of 8.2 per cent, the lowest rate registered in over a year.
Because our labour force has been growing much more rapidly than in other industrialized countries-since 1970 about 3'/2 per cent a year, compared to 2 per cent for the U.S., under 1 per cent for the U.K., France and Japan, and a decline for Germany-unemployment has reached very high levels, despite the rapid increase in the number of Canadians who are working. Employment increased by more than 3.6 per cent in the last year, and 362,000 more Canadians are working today than one year ago.
One of the main reasons for the fast growth of the labour force is the rapidly growing participation of Canadian women in the labour force.
Another important reason for the growth of the labour force has been a surge of young people coming into the labour market. This surge is not expected to last. The population in the 15 to 19-year-old age group is expected to decline after 1979. However, the immediate challenge has been to create enough jobs for all our young people and to alleviate other structural unemployment problems.
In the field of manpower-training and job creation, the government has recently announced an employment strategy for 1979-80 which continues the key objective of increasing the employment and employability of all Canadians, while shifting the emphasis to helping industry train and employ Canadians, and particularly young job seekers.
A main feature of the 1979-80 employment strategy is the development of a strategy to increase youth employment, particularly in the private sector, at a cost of $225 million. The summer youth employment program will be expanded, which includes programs such as Young Canada Works, Summer Job Corps, and so on. Expenditures will be increased on year round youth employment and employability programs, Youth Job Corps-a new program-job experience training, and so on, from $14.5 million this fiscal year to nearly $110 million in 1979-80. It is expected that the JET program alone will provide private sector employment and experience to over 63,000 youth in 1979-80.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order with respect to starred questions and their status in parliament. I first brought this topic up in February, 1975. At that time I inquired about a question which had not been answered for approximately a month. Your answer on this point, sir, was that there was no way which you knew of by which you could enforce an answer on the particular question.
I would like to go over the history of the starred question and to say that I am fighting this case because of your position, sir, as well as the position in which it puts every member in this House, no matter on which side they sit. The starred question goes back to the time when the nation of Canada was formed. At that time the rules and regulations came from the Mother of Parliaments at Westminster.
During the Confederation Parliament of 1867 questions were put only on the order paper, and there were no oral questions or starred questions. It was not until members began to get fractious, as they do here occasionally, and were asking questions, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the only pure blooded French prime minister that we have had, in 1910 brought in the policy of putting an asterisk behind the question on the order paper instead of asking oral questions, because they were becoming too obstructive. The rule he introduced was that an

November 22, 1978

asterisk would be put beside the question on any given day, and the following day that question would be answered.
It was not until the years 1929 to 1955 that starred questions were no longer put on the order paper. It was the Liberal government under Mr. St. Laurent that saw the wisdom of the starred question and had the procedures committee meet, which you and I have asked for several times, to try to establish the status of the starred question as one of the important procedures of our parliamentary system. At that time one of the speakers ruled that a starred question had to be answered.
As you know, custom dictates what this parliament does over the years. There is an idea prevalent among the newer members of this House, however, that a starred question need not be answered by a minister and may be left to fade away. I think Your Honour will agree that far too many questions are left on the order paper today.
In 1955, in order to speed things up, the Liberal government under Mr. St. Laurent saw fit to establish the status of the starred question. When I came here in 1957 it was a very well known fact that a question was to be answered within a period of seven days or less. Otherwise the minister of whom the question was asked was to get in touch with the member and ask for more time. I understood that to be a courtesy, that the question might be deferred for an answer, but we see it happening every day now. A question requiring a little more research was starred for the minister. In the United Kingdom they have two days, but under Sir Wilfrid Laurier we had one day.
It all goes back to the efficiency of parliament. Some members recently elected may find it difficult to catch Your Honour's eye or even to get up and ask a question, so it is much simpler for them to put it in written form. Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated that one of the reasons for doing this was to give a member the opportunity to bring up something of particular concern to his riding but not necessarily to the Dominion of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce today that, based on conclusions of one of the most thorough evaluations of a defence procurement program ever carried out in this country, cabinet has now approved a set of directions regarding the next

stage of the process towards acquisition of a new fighter aircraft for the Canadian Forces.
In arriving at these conclusions I have been guided by, and the judgments reflect, the military advice which I have received from the Chief of the Defence Staff. The finalists will be the General Dynamics CF-16 and the McDonnell-Douglas/Northrop CF-18A, which are the Canadian versions of these aircraft. The government has also decided against further consideration of a mixed fleet of fighters. The governments of the Federal Republic of Germany, Great Britain, Italy and United States, which all have been following this selection process with keen interest, are also being informed of this development.
Direction has now been given to the interdepartmental program office to initiate discussions leading to the negotiation of draft contracts with the two prime manufacturers remaining in competition. In addition to the very important questions of aircraft capability, fleet size, delivery schedule, and optimum phasing of payments, emphasis will be placed on negotiating the best mix of industrial benefits for Canada. In these negotiations particular attention will be paid to arrangements that could contribute to the growth of research and development activity in Canada, as well as high technology industry which complements our geography and resources. Emphasis also will be given to ensuring that all regions of the country will have full opportunity to participate in this program.
I expect that it will be several months before I am in a position to present a comparative analysis of draft contracts to cabinet for final selection of a new fighter aircraft. I am sure that those of you who have followed the evolution of the program since its start, in March, 1977, have come to realize the magnitude of the task facing the government in this selection process. At the end of June, as you will recall, the government decided to allow additional time to permit manufacturers to refine their initial proposals. I am pleased to report that by the new deadline of August 1 all had responded with offers that contained substantial improvements over their earlier proposals.
Our numerical requirement of between 130 and 150 aircraft is critical to our capability to meet our domestic and European commitments. We are indeed disappointed that procurement of sufficient numbers of F-14s, F-15s or Tornados could not be accommodated within our set budget of $2.34 billion in August 1977 dollars.
Our evaluation also revealed that acquisition of a mixed fleet would bring little or no benefit in terms of fleet size and that operation of such a fleet would bring substantial liabili-
National Defence
ties, including double training and logistics support systems over the life span of the aircraft.
The two most severe constraints that we face, and will continue to face, are the number of aircraft required and the set amount of money to buy them. Our task, then, is to buy the best military aircraft available within those constraints, while seeking the best possible industrial benefits with a minimum of project risk.
In addition to cost and numbers, there are other considerations that serve to favour the two aircraft we have kept in the process. To begin with, there is the military and political assessment that we have made of the current-and to a certain extent, anticipated-strategic situation that we are facing.

Having eliminated the three most expensive systems from the competition, three remained-the CF-16, the CF-18A and the CF-18L-that met or came very close to meeting our numerical requirements within the budgetary envelope while being able to meet the most likely military challenges.

Mr. Speaker, the arrangement made in 1973 was an arrangement with wheat producers that for seven years there would be a certain range within which the returns to them might move in connection with wheat sold for consumption in Canada. That range was originally set between a floor of $3.25 and a ceiling of $5. What we are now proposing is to raise the floor to $4 having regard to changes in the costs of production, and to allow the price to float in that range.
In 1973, because there had already been a very rapid escalation in the price of wheat to the $3 level and through that figure, the government decided to cushion the immediate impact of the rise by paying a consumer subsidy effective on everything over $3.25. That has gone on for some five years, to the benefit, I believe, of consumers to the extent of some $385 million. Now the government has decided that its spending restraint program requires this to be reviewed. Therefore, the cost-which perhaps would have been a cost to the treasury of $100 million this year-will now be changed in terms of a non-spending item and the Wheat Board will be free to make such a charge as the world price would indicate between the $4 and $5 range, which is a continuation of the old agreement.

November 29, 1978
Oral Questions
While there will be an unfortunate, but necessary, increase in the price of bread, it should be recognized that it follows five years of complete stability in the part of the bread price which represents wheat. Other factors have gone up, of course, and the price of bread has continued to rise over that period- but not because of wheat. January 23, 1979

Apart from the Official Languages Act, we have seen the labelling legislation and the broadcasting policy designed to spread two languages across the land, whether or not they are wanted or needed. I would suggest the metric system is also being forced on this country at great cost and dislocation to many parts of the economy, for the same reason. We have even heard of French being used in answering consular telephones in Australia.
Of course the Liberal party is not the only party striving to give Canada a French accent. We have the efforts of the Progressive Conservative party to change our ways in this very chamber to correspond to the ways of France. I refer, of course, to the practice of clapping which was introduced by the Progressive Conservatives in this chamber last fall. It is interesting to note where this practice originated, and in this connection I should like to refer to the Montreal Gazette issue of Wednesday, December 15, 1976, in which appeared the story about the new national assembly which was elected there on November 15 of that year.

The applause itself marked another change in style introduced by the Parti Quebecois, complementing a slow conversion from British to French parliamentary tradition.
Government MNAs clapped their hands to exhibit approval instead of thumping their desk tops, a practice adopted from France's national assembly whose name was appropriated by the Quebec legislature under the Union Nationale government of Daniel Johnson.
My concern is that the efforts of the Government of Canada to turn our nation into a country which would entitle it to attend a Francophone summit or Commonwealth conference would be akin to the old saw about the great surgeon who was asked about the results of one of his heroic procedures, to which he replied that of course the operation was a great success but unfortunately the patient died.
I therefore call upon the government to cease its efforts to change the ways of our country by trying to force feed its misconceived ideas about language and culture on an unwilling population.

The point I should like to make is that there are problems with the estimates procedure, but the problems do not necessarily emanate from the front benches of either side of this House. A lot of problems emanate from the back benches on both sides of this House. It is something which the government and opposition parties must look after, for this is not something which was imposed upon backbenchers by the government. It is something which has developed over a period of time. We should pay more attention to these things, rather than blabber on about useless motions such as the one before us today.
I am concerned about the manner in which we have proceeded with our procedural debates. The hon. member for Yukon made a totally absurd statement when he said that there has been no review of procedural changes. This is an absolute falsehood. Anybody who has been around the House of Commons for the last two and one half years and who has paid attention to what has been going on in the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, who has taken the trouble to pull out those volumes and to read them, would know what absolute bafflegab that is.
I have in my hand the proceedings of those committees. 1 had the honour to be the chairman of the subcommittee on the use of time. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was the chairman of the subcommittee on committees, and my parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane), was the chairman of the subcommittee on private members' hour. We met for a period of one year. We went to England to study their system, we had hearings, and we even met when the House was not sitting, in order to consider the reports which were worked on by these bodies.
It was no surprise to me that the members in the Conservative party, members who have paid a great deal of attention to this kind of problem, such as the hon. member for Edmonton

West, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath)-none of whom are in the House at the present time-had the common sense and courtesy not to sign such a ridiculous motion.
I would like to deal with some of the charges made by the hon. member for Yukon. I am concerned about the way in which he has distorted the historical facts. I think it is clear that these reforms, when they began, did not immediately appear out of the blue. The process started with Mr. Pearson's government in 1963. It was started in 1963 because the Conservative backbenchers, under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), were totally dissatisfied with the way in which parliament was carried on and with their particular role, and so were members on this side. When the latter became the government they decided to do something about it.
A series of committees was set up and a series of experiments was carried out, culminating in the changes of 1968 to 1969. How are those changes accepted? They were accepted unanimously, without a dissenting vote, and there was not even an "on division." Those rules were not rammed down the throats of the opposition. For those members who may not wish to accept that statement at face value, I would advise them to look at the Debates and Journals of the House of Commons for December 20, 1968. They were adopted without opposition. I will not bore the House by repeating the substance of those rules, but perhaps I should remind hon. members of the result of those rules with respect to supply.
The several standing committees in the House now spend over 500 hours a year studying main and supplementary estimates, more than twice as long as was spent under the old rules in the committee of suppy on the floor of the House. That time, even though it is not spent as well as I would like to see, is surely spent far more effectively than it was on the floor of the House. If anybody doubts that, all they need do is to go back and take a look at the debates in the good old days and contrast them with even the worst committee hearings to find that there is more substance in committees today than there was in committees of the whole in the good old days.
There has been a significant improvement. It has opened up changes which allow hon. members to be more effective, and furthermore it has given them opportunities to get away from the leader syndrome which this House has always had, and has given ordinary members on both sides a greater role to play. I think we should be grateful for that.
Nobody claims that the system is perfect. Certainly I am one of those who claims that the system is in dire need of a good shakeup. As a result, after the 1974 election, the then president of the privy council and House leader, Mitchell Sharp, took on the chairmanship of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. We undertook a number of experiments, co-operatively, with members opposite, to find out how we could change the rules to make the situation more equitable and meet some of the criticisms that had been launched by members opposite. It is a rule imposed by members themselves at the request of members opposite. There is a great desire on the part of members on all sides of the House to see themselves as equal, and therefore they proceeded to make sure they had equal access to the floor of the committee. Hon. members have big egos, Mr. Speaker, but some members will have to decide to give way to other members of their party. December 5, 1978

up the committee system will have to make some difficult decisions. Again, it is a question of attitude.
I have been in this House almost as long as the hon. member for Yukon, Mr. Speaker, and can recall when the House of Commons used to keep more regular hours. I can also recall when parliament basically sat part-time. A session began in February, we took a break for Easter, and returned until June. If the House sat in the autumn, that was an unusual event.
In recent years we have gone to the opposite extreme. In over 13 years in the House I have seen us adjourn for the summer on the planned date only three times-in 1967, 1971, and 1978. The leader of the House held the same post on those three occasions, but I have to temper my congratulations to him. I recall that he also held that position in 1971 when the Christmas adjournment began on New Year's Eve and there was no Easter adjournment.
If parliament is to be a year-round institution, then its members will have to organize their lives in a reasonable manner. In my judgment, this means that we will have to adopt regular sitting periods that would be extended only in cases of genuine emergency.
Let us look at the implications of this. It would put the government of the day, of whatever party, in a most awkward position. The present rules would give it no guarantee that it would be able to have a decision on its legislative program. We cannot establish a system where, on the other hand, however, the government would be able to ram a huge legislative program through without parliament giving it the proper attention. That would be unwise, and I certainly would not recommend it to the House.
In the last 15 years, experience has shown that between 50 and 70 bills must be passed and are passed each year. As a veteran member, and a minister with perhaps what is a small and controllable department, I believe that proper planning and control, from cabinet level down through the public service, could easily reduce this number to 40 or 50 bills per year. I would remind the House that the government has shown some signs of improving this in the last few years.
If a legislative program of a reasonable size is to be dealt with in a limited period of time, then planning is obviously required on both sides of the House. After all, we are all human, and if we do not have incentives to make us plan, then obviously we will not do it.
I should like to propose some things that we might consider. First of all, the rules regarding management of the time of the House should require the government to produce the great bulk of its legislative program early in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. This would enable the opposition to evaluate the bills and establish its position. This, it seems to me, would be a considerable reform. I am not talking about a list of bills-I mean the actual legislation as drafted.
Parliament
Second, representatives of all parties should be able to discuss the amount of time needed for measures and agree on packaging groups of bills, or batching, if you will. We could put them into categories, for instance, major, minor, controversial, and dull, for consideration within set period of time at specified stages.
Third, some device for the government to proceed unilaterally in cases where agreement is impossible must be retained. However, my judgment, and the recommendation made by our committee on the use of time, was to head toward the British system of giving the Speaker greater authority in accepting or rejecting unilateral time limitation proposals. I am prepared to admit that we may have to seek another way because of the nature of this particular House.
Finally, I would not apply the packaging proposals to the third reading stage of major bills. It seems to me that in cases of great controversy, at the final stage the government should be willing, ready and able to take its responsibilities fully and openly. Old-fashioned closure would be the only medicine in these cases, and the government would have to take that decision along with the kudos and the problems that that brings.
The motion before us today is really an admission of failure on the part of the hon. member for Yukon who had not done his homework, had not read his debates, had not read his committee reports, and had not participated in the committee reports. The opposition is saying, through the hon. member for Yukon, that we cannot do our job, that it is the system that is to blame. Quite frankly, if I had been a minister of longer standing than I am now, I think the government could say that too from time to time. I am prepared to say that the truth lies somewhere in between. It is neither black nor white; it is probably gray. After 13 years of being enmeshed in the committee system as it has developed, I am not prepared to say it is perfect. As one of the participants in the design of some of these aspects of it, I find there is a great deal that ought to be changed, but a lot of that could be changed by the members themselves if they wish to change.
However, what I do insist upon is that we deal with the question of attitude of hon. members. There is no shortage of good ideas for reform in this place, but what there is, Mr. Speaker, is a shortage of determination on the other side to grasp the opportunities that are available to them.

You had to be
heard by the sound of your own voice. Many members tried it once and did not try again. I notice now that if the electricity goes off this place comes to a standstill.
When I first came here, I sat in the back row. There was no electronic equipment of any kind. I had to be heard by the sound of my own voice. It was nicer for some of us. In our party we all seemed to have good voices. At least we had lots of nerve, or whatever it took, and we were all participants. However, the two old parties seemed to have 25 or 50 milquetoasts. They would make one speech in the session and find it so difficult to be heard that they gave up. That was fine for us.
We did not get caught in these quotas as to time. We were able to make all the speeches we wanted to make. But I think this is a better parliament because there is more participation. It is better not just because of television but because of the microphones that were brought in here. That innovation made more of a change in parliament than anything I have seen since I have been here, even more than television. Once the microphones were brought in, they produced an equality in terms of being heard. From that day on, the participation by all members has increased greatly. In that sense, it is a better place than it used to be.
In terms of the rules, we have made a number of changes which make this a better place. I like what we did with regard
December 5, 1978

to statements by ministers which we used to call statements on motions. That is not the correct term now. It is statements on statements.
In the old days, every time a minister made a statement there had to be an argument as to whether anybody had a right to reply and, if so, how many. There were no questions. We resolved that. We provided, by rule, that when a minister makes a statement one spokesman from each party can reply and there can be a question period. It may have reduced the number of statements that are made, but the handling of those statements is much better under the present rule than it was under the old.
The institution of "the late show" was beneficial to the operation of this place. Under the old system, members got put down when their questions were out of order. They had to wait for months for some grievance spot to raise something. With the institution of "the late show," if a member is not satisfied with an answer in the question period, it is possible to get on one of nine spots during the week after ten o'clock. I have noticed in changes in the rules that have been made since "the late show" was introduced that it has not been abolished. I think the Chair likes it as well. Mr. Speaker knows that if he puts a member down, that member has a right to get on "the late show".
We have improved our handling of legislation by the method of sending bills, with the exception of tax bills, to a standing committee, then establishing as we did the report stage. Back in the so-called good old days, all bills were dealt with here in committee of the whole. On occasion we would send a bill to a committee. If we did that, when it came back to committee of the whole, we went over it again. Usually members on the standing committee learned something about the bill while it was in progress. When it came back to committee of the whole, they could talk longer than if it had not been to the standing committee. I can give you chapter and verse. It happened quite often.
We now send bills to a standing committee, but we have the report stage here. At the report stage we do not have every clause called as we did in the old committee of the whole set-up. Instead members have to put down their amendments to specific clauses in the bill. In other words, the rights of hon. members who are not on the standing committee are reserved. They can deal with the parts of the bill they are concerned with here on the floor of the House.
In many of these respects, this place has improved. The introduction of television and radio broadcasting of the proceedings of this House is good. We get a lot of complaints. One of the biggest complaints last year was that people did not like the desk thumping. The Tories have tried to correct that by applauding, using their hands. We will have to wait a while to see what the Gallup poll says as to which people like, thumping desks or clapping hands.
The odd thing is that even though people criticize parliament from what they see over television, they seem to want more of it. The broadcasting people tell us there is more and more demand for the question period and other parts of this
Parliament
show to appear over television. I am told it even upstages some of the soap operas during the day. That did not happen in the good old days. I think this is good.
I could go on. I welcome the points that the hon. member across the way made about the opportunities of the facilities that are made available to members to do their job. When I came here, we were given a railway pass which we could use as often as we wanted. We still get it. We got our berth and meals, our expenses for making trips home by train. How often? Twice a year. Now we get 52 air trips a year. Don't tell me about the good old days.

the projects lacked proper control of the way the money was being spent. In instance after instance he found that the taxpayers' money was being spent unwisely and that value for money was not received.
He noted that at the time these 13 capital works projects were approved by parliament their estimated value was going to be $281,600,000, but by the time these 13 projects were finished the cost to the taxpayer was some $699,700,000. The cost had more than doubled. The Auditor General concluded in this part of the study that the absence of appropriate controls calls in question not only the $10 billion capital cost of current projects, but also operating and maintenance commitments that stretch decades into the future.

The parrots opposite insist on speaking about the McDonald royal commission. Something the members of the government do not realize is that the privileges of this House are the responsibility of members of this House and not of the McDonald royal commission. It is time members opposite learned that lesson. It explains why, when there is embarrassing or potentially damaging information, the authorities go
December 6, 1978

to almost any length to conceal it. It explains why the government fears to proceed with an open information law which would be effective in providing members of this party, members of this House, and members of the public, with an opportunity to find out what is the truth.
Let me use another illustration. I mentioned the public. What about the case involving the Toronto Sun! The Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) told us how he toiled, sweated, and strove mightily for 17 hours to examine 17,000 documents. Out of those 17,000 documents he extracted 580 odd and said those documents must be covered by section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act. He swore an affidavit that he had personally examined them and that, in his opinion as an officer of the Crown and as Solicitor General, those documents should not be made public.
What we have seen demonstrated by the facts established by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham is that we cannot rely on statements such as that made by the Solicitor General. 1 am not saying that he personally may not have believed that, but the information upon which he swore that affidavit resulted in 500 odd documents not being produced in the trial of the Toronto Sun and Peter Worthington. Reputable counsel in that case said those documents were essential in order to conduct an adequate defence. The Solicitor General said no, they were not. How can the court in that case, and the accused, rely on that affidavit which unfortunately, as the law now exists, cannot be appealed? It is binding. It is mandatory. Under those conditions, surely any reasonable, rational, intelligent person must have great doubts about the quality of that affidavit sworn by the Solicitor General and filed with the court in the Official Secrets Act case against Peter Worthington and the Toronto Sun.

Who are they who might be tempted to vote against this motion? I cannot name them, but they are those who wish to perpetuate the cover-up, the stonewalling, the delay and the whole litany of procedures the government has

practised for months respecting the broader issue of security service operations which led to the setting up of the McDonald commission. Ample evidence regarding that issue has been forthcoming for months now, not just in this debate. There have been questions during question periods, speeches and questions of privilege for months and months.
At first there was supposed to be one isolated incident. Then there was contradictory evidence, and we went on and on. There was an attempt to cover up. Prima facie cases having been established, there have been only two incidents since, I believe, 1965 in which government members voted against sending matters to committee. It is a remarkable coincidence that those two instances related to this particular issue. One would have to be very naive to believe that that is coincidence.
Who else might be tempted to vote against this motion? There are those who wish to have the executive proceed without accountability to the highest court of this country, this parliament. In the interests of expediency and efficiency there might be some who would say that executive action need not be accounted for to anyone. I believe that is the philosophy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It has been the philosophy of many political leaders, none of whom were very successful over the long run and most of whom were regretted in terms of history. However, that philosophy appears to be very much the philosophy of this government.
It has been said that ministers should be expected not only not to know about day to day operations but that they should virtually and deliberately avoid knowing. That is one of the most outstanding statements I have ever heard in terms of its repugnancy to me. It is absolutely unacceptable in terms of all I have come to know about parliamentary democracy. It is unacceptable by any yardstick because its logical extension would be that there should be government by the executive branch alone. I cannot accept that.
Nor can 1 accept the establishment by the executive of a special agency to examine the executive, such as the McDonald commission, as a replacement for accountability to parliament. With all its inefficiencies, with all its lack of expediency and with all the frustrations there may be, accountability to parliament has been the best system ever devised. If someone can show me a better system which eliminates the need for having the executive account for its actions and which at the same time protects the interests of the people it is set up to serve, then I would be the first to change my mind; but for centuries of parliament the fact that such a system exists has never been successfully argued.
Finally, there will be a group which might be tempted to vote against this motion. This group would be those who wish the rights and privileges of members to take second place to political expediency and political cover-up. Now, sir, in a pre-election period, as we all know, atmospheres change, attitudes change, performances change. That is part of the system. But that does not mean that one changes one's integrity. It does not have to mean that one compromises one's principles.
December 7, 1978

It does not have to mean that the very root of parliamentary democracy, that of accountability, has to take second place. Even from the crassest, most partisan political viewpoint, I cannot understand why we would deny a committee the right to investigate what Mr. Speaker calls a deliberate attempt to obstruct a member. Once it is found to be a prima facie case that there was a deliberate attempt to obstruct a member-and Mr. Speaker found that that was the only conclusion to which he could come-the only conclusion was that there was a deliberate attempt to mislead; it was not negligence, carelessness or an inadvertent act, but a deliberate attempt to mislead and obstruct a member.

Parliament will be asked to deal with alleged misuse of social insurance numbers, says Human Rights Commissioner Gordon Fairweather.
