It would be helpful to know the true purpose of the motion. It might be that the motion flows from either a concern that the government's contracting systems are not open or accessible, or possibly from recent comments by the Auditor General on contracting in government. First, I would like to deal with possible concerns about openness in the contracting activities of the government, and in particular within the Department of Supply and Services.
Openness in the contracting system of the Department of Supply and Services is achieved through a wide dissemination of relevant contracting information to the Canadian public. This policy of openness is a further good reason why the requested contract documents need not be tabled. In order to understand fully how openness with respect to contracting information is achieved, it is first necessary to understand the role of DSS in contracting, which I will describe. In addition, it will be necessary to cover the responsibilities and procedures for contracting in so far as DSS is involved. Then I will describe the mechanisms used to provide all relevant DSS contracting information to the Canadian public. I will conclude with examples of the significant benefits achieved by the current availability and provision of contracting information to the public, which will underscore the lack of necessity for tabling all contracts for the year 1976-77.
The Department of Supply and Services provides a wide range of services to other federal government departments and agencies. The department is divided into two sections: supply administration and services administration. The services administration is responsible for the distribution of the cheques issued by the federal government, including payroll, pension and family allowance cheques. In addition, it is responsible for accounting, audit and management advisory services within the federal government. The supply administration is responsible for the procurement of everything from typewriters to tanks and ships for the federal government, buying about $3 billion worth of goods and services in 1976-77 alone.
Besides procurement, the supply administration is responsible for the provision of such other common services as printing and publishing, traffic management, warehousing and distribution, and expositions. Reporting to the Minister of Supply and Services and working closely with the supply administration is the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation which is responsible for the sale of surplus goods to the public.
The supply administration's prime objective is to provide or obtain the goods and services essential to government programs at a fair and reasonable price and, at the same time, to ensure prudence and probity in the expenditure of public funds and an equal opportunity for Canadian business and industry to do business with the federal government.
Government Contracts
As I have mentioned, one of the major impediments to tabling copies of all contracts is the sheer volume of documentation. I will give a description of the contracting responsibilities and procedures in order to indicate the complexities involved which, in turn, are reflected in contract documentation.
In a general way, the supply administration operates in a similar fashion to a supply organization within a major firm in that it is part of a larger corporation, that is, the federal government, and the basic services provided are similar. However, with close to $3 billion of annual buying power, the sheer magnitude and diversity of government operations places the supply administration in a unique position with respect to private sector supply operations. In this respect the supply administration's prime objectives are, first, to obtain the goods and services essential to government programs at a fair and reasonable price, while at the same time, second, to ensure prudence and probity in the expenditure of public funds, and third, to provide an equal opportunity to all Canadians to do business with the federal government on a fair and reasonable basis.
In the contracting process, these objectives are achieved through a judicious sharing of responsibilities between the supply administration and its customer program departments. For example, a policy has been developed which delegates low dollar value contracting responsibilities to customers, and there are provisions which allow customers the necessary flexibility to conduct emergency purchasing, where appropriate. Aside from this, some aspects of services contracting are a customer department's responsibility, although the supply administration does conduct a wide range of services contracting.
Within the contracting mandate of the supply administration, the actual process of purchasing can, and frequently does, involve much more than issuing tenders and evaluating bids. It begins with the identification of an operational need by a customer department, the funding for which must be provided for in the department's annual main estimates submission.

The hon. member says, "Let's try it", but I am personally not prepared to take the chance of losing some of the most able people in the country on this issue of remuneration. I think the Canadian people are prepared to pay according to responsibility assumed.

As we know, federal administrations in the United States change every four years. The difference is that people who assume the roles of undersecretaries, assistant undersecretaries and others in terms of the policymaking apparatus in the United States are essentially servants of the people during limited periods of time. It is a responsibility and an honour to take such positions, but these people are basically private sector people who return to the private sector at the end of a given four-year period. Some of them take leaves of absences from universities, businesses and so forth. In fact, in many respects I suggest that that aspect of the U.S. system is healthy because there is a constant interchange between private sector and public sector personnel due to this process.
There are very few major law firms, investment houses or corporations in the United States which do not have among their ranks some people who have served government in senior capacities in one or more administrations. Unfortunately-and I say "unfortunately" because our system as it now operates is not compatible with that kind of change-we have basically a permanent civil service in this country. There are great advantages and disadvantages to our system, but I suggest that in the absence of undertaking very fundamental reforms in the entire government apparatus in Canada it would be virtually impossible to adopt this motion at this time. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this private members' bill I suppose I should begin by pointing out the agreement which we on this side of the House have with the author of this bill in that good ideas from all corners of the House are always acceptable. We are very interested in examining suggestions for improvements to the legislation of Canada whether emanating from private members or the government. That sentiment is obviously one which is shared not only by the author of this bill and by members on this side of the House but also, indeed, by the government. It is quite possible to say that all of the good ideas the government has had for the last ten years have come from this side of the House to begin with.
There are a number of things about this bill, however, which, once we get past the principle of being willing to examine any suggestion, occur to me. The first is that this bill purports to amend the British North America Act. I may have been labouring under some sort of delusion for the last 35 years, but it is my understanding that one of the greatest problems facing Canada today is the difficulty of amending the British North America Act.
We have been trying for close to 50 years to amend the British North America Act and we have been unable to agree on exactly how to do it. Here is a private member's bill from a distant corner of the House which purports in four or five

paragraphs to do it. I find that strange. I would not suggest that it is arrogant. I do not think any private members opposite are arrogant. Arrogance is a very special kind of disease, and the carriers opposite are restricted to a certain number of seats. However, if one sits too close to the carrier of a disease, sometimes the spores may be borne on the wind and one can be infected. I would not make that accusation; I merely suggest that it is possible in this case that the author of this bill may have got the idea that with a private member's bill he could do what the government of this country has been unable to do, despite all its efforts, for the past ten years.

The purpose of this bill is to fix at four years the duration of every House of Commons notwithstanding any successful "no confidence" motion. If a minority government suffered a defeat on what is traditionally accepted as a "no confidence" matter, there would be required the development of a convention of the constitution which would enable a government to carry on until the day fixed for a general election.
I remember a movie a few years ago entitled, I think, "Carry on Regardless," which it seems to me is what is being suggested here: carry on despite having lost the confidence of the House of Commons; carry on despite having been defeated.
In proposed section 50(3) of the act there is provision for a government to be defeated on a motion for the approval of its budgetary policy, a motion to concur in main estimates or a motion expressing lack of confidence, so perhaps that covers that objection; but it seems to me somewhat fundamental to our system of parliamentary democracy that one of the few protections the people of the country have is that, if the government is defeated in this chamber, it must resign and ask for a new mandate. It is verging on the outrageous to suggest that that be altered. One of the fundamental protections in our system is our ability to dismiss the government.
In another clause of the bill it is suggested that there be a ceremonial gathering, a pretty ceremony, once a year on or about July 1 at which there would be participation by representatives of the different walks of life and ethnic and religious communities in Canada. Surely it is not going too far to suggest that that is what we already have in this chamber. It is the entire purpose and foundation of this chamber that we be representative of the different walks of life and ethnic, religious, social, political and geographic communities in Canada. I would have no objection, in a ceremonial sense, to adding other representation to this body on one day of the year. I think it might be instructive, for example, to have our friends in the fourth estate come down from their special perch for a while, but I am not sure that would get directly at what the hon. member is suggesting in this bill.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to contribute a few words to the debate this afternoon. One of the underlying principles of this bill is to provide additional funding to the government for constructive job creation and training programs. This bill and other government funding would provide some $710 million for this purpose in the coming fiscal year, part of which would derive from the savings realized by the operation of the unemployment insurance program.
The opposition has explored this bill in great detail in committee. There were some 35 committee meetings, and all the amendments presented for consideration at report stage were dealt with in considerable detail at those meetings.
The opposition obviously has responsibility to oppose a bill and to make positive and constructive amendments to it, but there must come a time when members from all sides can vote. We can either have continued blockage or obstruction of a bill, or else it comes to a vote.
A motion under Standing Order 75C allows the government to set a time limit on debate, and provides that report stage and third reading can be dealt with in the same motion. In this case two sitting days have been proposed to deal with report stage and third reading. That would bring us up to two days before Christmas when I think many members will be getting away for the recess and all members will want to get back to their constituencies.
Allotment of Time for Bill C-14
As I recall, when changes were made to the rules in 1969, the idea was that the policy of a bill would be explored on second reading, it would be sent to committee for clause by clause study, then be dealt with at report stage and proceed for expeditious third reading. In the case before the House it is clear that the opposition, or at least the NDP, did not want to bring the bill to a vote but rather wanted to prolong discussion indefinitely. This bill would provide additional funding for direct employment programs and direct skill training programs and, surely, that is what most people in this country want. I receive many letters and communications, as I am sure other members do, asking why we spend so much money on welfare and unemployment insurance benefits and why we do not put people to work, and provide more training that would equip them for jobs.
This bill would make expanded job creation and training programs available to the government, Mr. Speaker. The program outlined by the minister at a cost of some $710 million for 1979-80 would do what many people want. It would provide 113,000 job-years of employment and activities, through such things as part-time jobs for students or on the job training in which 368,000 people could participate. This is a 70 per cent increase in work-years over previous figures.
I am especially interested in the fact that a lot of the emphasis is on youth employment, because often young persons coming out of high schools or post-secondary institutions cannot get jobs as they do not have experience on the job. They have not held jobs and have no letters of reference from previous employers. This program has a strong emphasis on youth with some $225 million for youth employment, some of which will come from savings through the UIC bill.
As a matter of fact, the job experience training program will be expanded from some 20,000 jobs to 63,000 jobs. This is for young people just coming directly out of school, and some $40 million will come from UIC benefits, creating a positive force for job training and job experience for young people, rather than being used as a direct pay-out from which we do not in the long term get any advantage for young people, such as experience on the job and becoming accustomed to being in the labour force. That does not occur when they are just drawing UIC benefits.
1 was also impressed by this job-creation program and the local economic development assistance program. We have in certain areas of the country local economic development corporations designed to seek out economic opportunities to create new businesses, but up until now there have been no equity funds available for this purpose. Often the banks are too tight-fisted, so there is no equity in the hands of the local entrepreneur who has a good idea and cannot put it together.
We have an economic development corporation in my constituency, and this program for local economic development assistance will provide some $10 million during the next fiscal year for the creation of about 1,000 permanent jobs.

December 20, 1978
Allotment of Time for Bill C-14
It seems to me that by implementing these programs designed to assist, stimulate, and provide an incentive to the private sector, we are looking at a much more positive way of utilizing the unemployment insurance funds that would be used in direct pay-outs if these positive and constructive programs were not available.
I am pleased to see that the minister is expanding by some 70 per cent these direct job creation and training programs. That is the real positive aspect of the move by the department to provide assistance to the private sector in order to fund direct employment programs.
In my constituency $1.5 million will be spent this year on direct job programs, providing jobs that will ultimately, at least some, move into the private realm. We have one project on an Indian reserve for the development of a new operation, a dolomite mine, an open-pit quarry that will create permanent jobs. This is being carried out through a Canada Works program.
It seems to me the question we have to ask ourselves is, do we want to continue pouring billions of dollars into UIC benefits, or do we want to use those funds to create employment for the native people and other unemployed? I think that is the direction in which the minister wants to move, and I would support him in that objective.

I understand why hon. members opposite are concerned about the size of the deficit next year. I understand why they feel that this is an area in which to save money. around the country, which is why we feel we cannot support the bill.
Members of the government and committee members who attended the hearings looked at the impact of the bill. Many, many times the terrible effects of this bill have been brought forward, but I should like to bring them out once more. At the present time there is an unemployment rate of 8.3 per cent seasonally adjusted as of last month. There are only four provinces below the average rate of unemployment, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The government's proposed measures will affect the provinces with low unemployment proportionately less severely than the provinces with high unemployment.
If one looks at the repeater and new entrants provisions, the proposed measures will affect 10 per cent of the unemployed in Newfoundland, 20 per cent in Prince Edward Island, 11 per cent in Nova Scotia, 12 per cent in New Brunswick, and 10 per cent in Quebec. In other words, the amendments will have maximum effect on areas with the highest rates of unemployment.
As several hon. members have pointed out, the 11.5 per cent relief rate for the repeater provision is a temporary salve. As the hon. member for St. John's East pointed out, Newfoundland and some of the other less-advantaged areas will be in terrible straits if they ever manage to bring down their unemployment rates below 11.5 per cent. As a result of the government's legislation and the new entrants and repeater provisions, if these areas manage to bring their unemployment rates below 11.5 per cent, the effects are just fantastic. I see why the government wants to cut off debate. It is because the bill cannot stand up to scrutiny. Even hon. members opposite recognize that it is a bad piece of legislation. Repeatedly members across the way have spoken against it.

obtained from a deposition given on behalf of the Boeing company in front of the SEC. To respond to the hon. member's question, the airworthiness directive requiring the removal of all ELTs powered by lithium batteries is still in force. As the status report on this subject shows, replacement battery packs (with no lithium batteries) are now available for approximately 90 per cent of the current emergency locator transmitter systems in operation. Once all battery packs can be replaced, the original air navigation order calling for installation (where applicable) of a functioning ELT in aircraft will be back in force.
I am sure the hon. member is very much aware of the need for removing lithium batteries from aircraft. There are documented cases indicating the danger of using this type of battery for ELTs, although fortunately, there were no casualties in any of the reported cases. It was decided that lithium batteries used in ELTs presented an unacceptable high risk for use in civil aircraft. Therefore, an airworthiness directive was issued ordering their immediate removal.
In view of the serious situation arising from the removal of ELTs, and cognizant of the safety factors that guide our ELT policy, it has been the objective of the Canadian Air Transportation Administration to restore ELTs to service as quickly as possible.
There is evidence now that no alternate lithium based call would be available or proven safe for civil aircraft application in the immediate future. Consequently, the seven manufacturers of ELTs, who hold Canadian type approval, were formally asked to submit a proposal for a program to retrofit their manufactured ELTs with a substitute non-lithium battery. Five of these companies have received approval for a battery retrofit program. They represent about 90 per cent of the ELT population. There is the potential that the majority of ELTs will be returned to service over the period extending into later this year.
Returning ELTs to service represents an interim phase in upgrading their effectiveness. But it should be pointed out that the ELT system will be deficient in at least two areas during this interim period. The modified ELT with a non-lithium battery will not meet the operating requirements of minus 40 degrees centigrade for 100 hours. The ELTs prior to their
Adjournment Debate
removal from the civil aircraft fleet were experiencing numerous technical problems other than those involving their batteries. These deficiencies will continue to affect over-all ELT proficiency.
Operational efficiency of ELTs is a North American problem which has precipitated intense activity in the industry. Lead times required for research and development, regulatory change and implementation, mean that it will be some time before the desired high performance of the ELT system can be realized.

I think it has been said here by some members that these 40 hours would be enough. That would justify setting aside this matter of the referendum intended by the federal government. Here, I refer, for instance, to page 2045 of Hansard of December 12, 1978, where a member was saying, and I quote:
If there is a particular referendum which we do not think is popular, the point is that we have the means in this House as an opposition to hold things up beyond the eight days. Indeed, if it happened that the government of the day, whether it be this government or any other, rammed through a referendum bill in the face of united opposition in the House of Commons, one does not have to guess what would happen. As I see it, Bill C-12 was intended to dispel both these fears. Even more to the point, I believe the bill will destroy the basis upon which some of these fears have grown- the distortions which have been placed in front of us all. I have been concerned for some ten or 12 years about the relationship of the government as an employer to its employees in the public service of Canada. On questions of pay and pensions perhaps it is time that the cabinet recognized that there is no longer a need for a direct relationship between the policy-making structure, the cabinet, and the employee. Perhaps it is time we began to examine the usefulness of an extended concept of the Treasury Board which allows it such authority and stature as to make it the employer, and not this parliament.
If we look to those areas of this country where there is a concentration of public servants, for whatever reason-perhaps it is the longevity of the present government; 15 or 16 years is perhaps too long for one group of individuals to lead effectively-we find that the majority of public servants are represented by members of this side of the chamber. I said that 85 per cent retire on pensions of less than $7,000 per year. I put that figure on the record last fall when the former president of the treasury board made his introductory remarks. Therefore it is important that these people receive more supplementation than those in the much higher categories. You will recall that last fall full indexing would have been allowed on earnings up to that $7,000 mark, and above that the figure in the proposal was 8 per cent in 1979, 7 per cent for 1980, and 6 per cent in 1981. However, because this particular bill did not pass last year, this item will

come up for review once again and later this year we will find out whether the amount is going to be around $7,500, or somewhere around $8,000 for full indexing. These figures are very familiar to me as I have many neighbours who have retired from the armed forces or the public service and find themselves in this particular pension income bracket.
Even though this debate today is related to pensions in the public sector, I feel, Mr. Speaker, that there is a real need to take a good look at some of the private pension funds as well. Ministers of labour at the provincial levels and the federal Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) should discuss the problems faced by those who do not have a portable pension plan, in this day and age. In today's world, we find people in their 30's and early 40's by necessity moving around to find other jobs. In many cases a person might have 18 years with one company but, because he is laid off his job, or his position has become redundant, and he has to find another source of employment, he or she may lose that 18 years in the pension plan, and simply be given the amount he or she placed in the fund. Many of these pension plans fall under provincial jurisdiction, but our federal Minister of Labour, who is a very humanitarian type, could do a lot of good for private citizens across this country if he were to initiate such meetings with the provincial ministers of labour in order to provide portability of pension plans for every Canadian citizen across Canada who spent a reasonable amount of time working for one particular company and then found it necessary to move or, indeed, saw a chance for promotion in another area.
Again I wish to return to discuss a very serious problem that today faces many of our military personnel who retire at an early age. In many cases the trades that personnel in the armed forces practised for many years are not recognized once they arrive out on "civvy street". In many cases provincial departments of labour refuse to license mechanics, plumbers, carpenters and so on without further apprenticeship training. As a result they find themselves on the labour market with no qualifications of a legal nature but they do have the experience and knowledge of their field. I have had many people in my office discussing this very subject.
At the present time there is a military-civilian training accreditation committee working on this problem, but it still has a long way to go; even though it has made a very good start. In view of the considerable lapse of time between the time a member of the armed forces is pensioned off and the time he will reach 60 years of age for indexing, and under present conditions the age of 65 for the old age security, it becomes very necessary to provide him with a legal recognition of his skills so he can supplement his income during those crucial years.
In the United States forces, they quite often use the last year of a military person's career, if it is their wish to do so, to train them for a job when they get out of the service. I can only strongly recommend to the Minister of National Defence that this type of program be seriously looked at by the
February 14, 1979

Department of National Defence in Canada, and also that he might solicit the support of our good friend, the Minister of Labour, to deal with the provinces on civilian accreditation for the skills that members of the armed forces already have.

The emphasis in any allocation program will be on practicality and simplicity in implementation. The Emergency Supplies Allocation Board will therefore have to seek the advice of oil companies. This may involve the companies in collective discussion of such advice to the board and in co-operative action. With this in view, special provision is made in the bill in case the companies are required-and I must emphasize the term "required"-to enter into agreements, arrangements or courses of action which might involve contravention of the Combines Investigation Act. The board may in those circumstances, by order, and only after consultation with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, exempt an applicant and such other persons as it deems necessary from the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, but only to the extent required to enable the applicant to comply with the allocation program.
The legislation empowers the board, in order to make better use of the available supplies of a controlled product, to make special regulations providing for a temporary relaxation of certain laws that currently restrict the emission of sulphur pollutants into the atmosphere. However, this would be done upon the issue of a short-term permit and only after consultation with the responsible ministers of the federal and provincial governments, for example, the departments of environment and health and welfare.
There are also provisions in the bill to enable the National Energy Board and the Canadian Transport Commission to co-operate with ESAB which will be co-ordinating programs in order to ensure that the petroleum products may be moved as directed by the board in order to relieve anticipated shortages.
Finally, this law will require the compulsory termination of a mandatory allocation program after 12 months, unless such a program is extended by the order of the governor in council with the approval of parliament. However, no such order may
Energy Supplies
extend the mandatory allocation program for longer than 12 months at a time. The bill requires that a motion to adopt an extension order be tabled in each House of Parliament within seven days after it has been made. If the House of Commons negatives the motion the allocation program shall thereupon terminate. We believe this is a better solution than the one that was worked out and included in the previous bill involving a sunset clause in which the whole legislation self-destructed in mid-1976.
I should like to say a word or two about federal-provincial industrial consultation which is a very important area. Allocation and rationing plans have been developed since 1974 by the original Energy Supplies Allocation Board and, since its demise, by officials of my department. These plans would form the basis of programs to be implemented by a recreated ESAB. They have been evolved as a result of extensive consultation with provincial governments, the petroleum industry and representatives of petroleum-consuming interests. I would expect this process of consultation to be continued by a new board. As I already indicated, membership of the board itself would reflect provincial, private consumer, and industrial interests. I am aware that allocation programs can only work effectively with broad public support. The board will, through consultation, seek such support and provincial co-operation.
Canada's energy needs are large in order to support our high standard of living, to deal with a cold climate, and to provide the transportation links across our broad land.
Canada's energy potential is great, and this government has worked long and hard to realize that potential. Let me give a few examples of this. The oil sands development is being encouraged by the payment of international prices for this product; by appropriate fiscal terms; and by direct participation in the Syncrude project where the federal government has a significant equity holding. Other important initiatives of the government include oil and gas exploration fostered by our pricing policies and by tax reliefs which specially assist pioneer efforts in frontier areas such as the Beaufort Sea.
The Canada-United States gas pipeline treaty opens the way for pipeline access to already discovered reserves in the McKenzie Delta. Petro-Canada, the bete noire of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), the major policy instrument in Canadian participation and government participation in industry, has become in three short years a major force in our petroleum industry, providing a stimilus to exploration, and participating in schemes for the expansion of eastern Canadian gas markets. I am referring to the gas pipeline which would move natural gas all the way to the maritimes, the bold plan to bring Arctic Islands gas to eastern Canada, liquefied natural gas from the high Arctic, using the Canadian system, and working to develop the heavy oils of western Canada.
The attitude of the Leader of the Opposition with respect to Petro-Canada was recycled last Friday, I believe, in Vancouver, when he said once again that he would dismantle Petro-Canada.

February 19, 1979
Energy Supplies

I was rather surprised last night to hear the hon. member for Nor-thumberland-Durham give the impression that it was somewhat shameful for Petro-Canada to be engaging in these international activities, that it was somewhat immoral, that is was a matter which should be left to the multinational corporations. We believe that this is a legitimate role for a national petroleum company which is operating in the public interest and in the interest of the people of Canada.
I am aware of the concern of residents of the Atlantic provinces, of consumers in Atlantic Canada and of provincial governments in Atlantic Canada about the region's heavy dependence on oil and about the fact that this oil is currently imported from potentially insecure foreign sources. I have just drawn attention to efforts being made by Petro-Canada to discover and develop the region's own petroleum resource potential, to substitute domestic gas for imported oil and to assure a higher degree of security for those imports which remain. Nevertheless, it is understandable that people in Atlantic Canada should look west and wonder whether and how they will be able to source at least a portion of their oil needs from discovered and developing resources in our own west.

The situation with respect to the acquisition of documents, as the hon. member will know, is that first of all in the House of Commons members may make application by way of a notice of motion for the production of documents. This is done on a regular basis and ministers, I am sure to the chagrin of opposition members, stand in their place and indicate that they are not going to produce their documents for various reasons.
If I were to grant that that matter were to become a question of privilege because the minister was refusing on some grounds to produce that document to a member, I think that I would be stretching the limit of the definition of privilege beyond recognition. If I were to decide that a prima facie refusal by a minister to produce a document became privilege, I would be altering the law or privilege considerably.
The hon. member does not actually say that he has made an application pursuant to motions for the production of documents and that the minister subsequently has refused to produce them. He does say in his argument that the minister has refused his other request for information, but he does not identify this particular one.
In addition, the hon. member supports his argument by referring to the fact that, if the document can be produced in a coroner's court, then it ought to be produced to the hon. member. That may very well be so, but it certainly does not follow that because the court has the power to subpoena a document, or have it produced to it or call as a witness the person who prepared the document, and thereby have access to the information, that that power necessarily lies in the hands of every member of parliament in the discharge of his obligations. Again, I think that it would be a considerable alteration of privilege to grant the hon. member's request.
If the hon. member has not already exhausted the other available devices open to him in securing this report, by way of a motion to produce the document, questions to the minister during question period and so on, I suggest that he ought to do so and perhaps in due time there may be more light shed on this argument. billion bushels of export. Well, we are now talking about a higher target than that.

Extensive authority was delegated to the Western Region without effective
